info.bio: Queen es una banda de rock clásico creada en Londres, Inglaterra en 1970. Su formación clásica fue liderada por el ya fallecido Freddie Mercury tras la ruptura del grupo Smile, banda de donde provienen Roger Taylor y Brian May en compañía de Tim Sttaffel. A mediados de 1971 se uniría como bajista John Deacon, quien se retiraría de la banda poco después de la muerte de Freddie. Actualmente la banda solo está conformada por Roger Taylor y Brian May.

scenes.desc: Tras la caída de P-Funk, muchos ritmos nuevos vinieron de fuera: Kraftwerk, Art of Noise («Beat Box», «Close (to the Edit)»), Talking Heads (Stop Making Sense, con Bernie Worrell) y el «Genius of Love» de Tom Tom Club. Herbie Hancock pidió a su mánager Tony Meilandt unos temas de hip hop y con Bill Laswell y Grandmixer D.S.T. hizo «Rockit» (Future Shock, 1983): la cima del funk industrial nada más empezar. Laswell (Material, Time Zone con John Lydon, Manu Dibango, los Last Poets) dejó su sello de bajo grueso; sellos como Celluloid, On-U Sound, Tommy Boy o Def Jam sacaban ritmos ásperos de raspados metálicos y tensión de Guerra Fría. On-U Sound de Adrian Sherwood fichó a la sección rítmica de Sugarhill (Doug Wimbish, Skip McDonald, Keith LeBlanc): Tackhead, el «No Sell Out» con la voz de Malcolm X, «el P-Funk de los ochenta» según Pedro Bell.

scenes.desc: El hard rock marca el fin de los creativos sesenta: sigue basado en el blues, pero más rápido, ruidoso y fuerte, y entierra el sufrimiento negro bajo miles de decibelios. Precedido por Cream, Blue Cheer y Guess Who, lo definen Led Zeppelin, hijos del blues que lo tocan como música para el cuerpo y que imponen el LP como formato del rock. En Gran Bretaña, Free, Status Quo, Thin Lizzy, UFO, Uriah Heep, Slade, Faces, Deep Purple (el estereotipo del género), Black Sabbath (cimientos del black y el doom metal) y Queen, los bromistas del movimiento. podcast.title: Union Rules and Video Innovation (1975)
podcast.body: Queen faced a significant hurdle with the British Musicians Union rules, which strictly prohibited lip-syncing on television. This made it impossible for them to perform their complex song "Bohemian Rhapsody" live on TV while maintaining its integrity. To circumvent these rules, they created the innovative "Bohemian Rhapsody" video, which became a landmark in music video history. "Why? Because the rules of the British Musicians Union prohibited lip syncing on TV."

podcast.title: News of the World (1977) - Album Cover Iconography
podcast.body: The iconic robot on the "News of the World" album cover is a nearly identical copy of a sci-fi fanzine from 1953. The original artist from the fanzine was commissioned by the band to create the cover, and also developed all the iconography within the album, including original paintings in the booklet depicting people screaming in terror from the robot, and related posters. This visual has been highly influential, inspiring reinterpretations in comics like X-Men and even a subtle nod in a Family Guy episode. "Realmente es una copia casi idéntica de un fancine de ciencia afición de 1953."

podcast.title: Jazz (1978) - Bicycle Race Nudism Controversy
podcast.body: The iconography surrounding the first single "Bicycle Race" was highly controversial. Freddie Mercury, inspired by a photograph of nude women in a race, wanted to base the single and album's visual theme on this. Due to censorship, the single cover could not show full nudity, so a small cropped image of a nude woman on a bicycle had panties drawn onto her. The original "Jazz" album versions included a small poster of the nude women's race, which was censored in countries like the United States, forcing Queen to remove it. To circumvent this, a coupon was included, allowing fans to mail away for the poster. Queen subsequently created extensive iconography around the nude cyclists, including posters, concert visuals, and merchandise. This visual theme was significant in the 1970s, an era when nudism was a form of protest against the connection between nudity and sexuality. "Esta fotografía, acabo siendo censurada en muchos países como Estados Unidos donde no podía mandarse fotos de desnudo."

podcast.title: Flash Gordon (1980) - Soundtrack Iconography
podcast.body: While the "Flash Gordon" soundtrack album is considered one of Queen's lower artistic moments, its iconography is fantastic. The band masterfully integrated their image with Flash Gordon's superhero iconography, creating numerous intriguing posters. This era produced one of Freddie Mercury's most iconic looks: wearing a Flash Gordon t-shirt, leather shorts, and famously pictured atop a Darth Vader figure. "Nos lejó uno de los momentos icónicos más maravillosos de Freddy Mercury con la camiseta de Flash Gordon, unos y ors de cuero subido encima de Darth Vader."

podcast.title: The Works (1984) - "I Want To Break Free" Videoclip
podcast.body: Creatively, "The Works" is one of Queen's most questioned albums, but it yielded the visually epic music video for "I Want To Break Free." The video features all band members in drag, famously including Freddie Mercury vacuuming while crossing a doorway. The humor and impact came from seeing other band members like Roger Taylor and Brian May in drag, breaking taboos prevalent in the 1980s. The video also contains other memorable moments, such as a scene interpreted as a version of ancient Greek bacchanalian feasts, showcasing a graphically interesting aesthetic. "Lo divertido no era a Freddy Mercury travestido, era a ver los a los otros."

podcast.title: A Kind of Magic (1986) - 80s Aesthetic
podcast.body: The "A Kind of Magic" album embodies the pure essence of the 1980s aesthetic. This period blended various stylistic factors, including influences from David Bowie's 80s photography. The title track's music video is an apotheotic moment where animation and music interact fantastically, and the album also includes the soundtrack for "Highlander," featuring the song "Who Wants to Live Forever," which also has a wonderful aesthetic moment. "Aquí se mezclan un montón de factores estéticos que hacen que la iconografía de Queen esta época se interés antísima."

podcast.body: The music video for "The Invisible Man" drew its inspiration from a video game, depicting the band members as video game characters, which was a very interesting visual concept. "Donde hacen un video clip inspirado en un videojuego donde ves a los personajes como videojobos."

podcast.title: The Miracle (1989) - Album Cover Technology
podcast.body: Although "The Miracle" is not always considered the most critically acclaimed album in Queen's career, its cover features a highly interesting graphic element: a single image blending the four faces of the band members. Created in 1989, this computer-generated composite was a technological marvel for its time, executed using the famous Quantel Paintbox, a precursor to Photoshop and other video editing programs. At the time, this advanced photographic editing technique was revolutionary, even if it seems unremarkable today. "Este dibujo que mezcla en una sola imagen las cuatro caras de los miembros de Queen es uno de los momentos interesantes desde el punto de vista gráfico y estamos hablando en 1989 y hacer esta especie de montajes fotográficos no era sencillo."

podcast.title: "I'm Going Slightly Mad" (1991) - Music Video Tribute
podcast.body: The music video for "I'm Going Slightly Mad" is almost a tribute to the band's history and a beautiful aesthetic moment. Freddie Mercury embodies a version of the protagonist from "The Rocky Horror Picture Show" and delivered one of his most iconic looks by wearing a banana wig. "Freddy Mercury es y versional, el protagonista de roche y horror picture show."

podcast.title: Innuendo (1991) - Graphic Complexity
podcast.body: "Innuendo" is arguably the most graphically and iconographically interesting point in Queen's entire career due to its complex visual language. The music video for the title track is a highly intricate collage of various elements, including film footage, animation, and old recordings, all perfectly synchronized with the music, faithfully reflecting the song's complexity. "Si el Inuendo musicalmente es complejo, visualmente también es muy complejo."

xref.title: "Today" Show Interview (1976) – National Controversy
xref.body: On Wednesday, December 1st, 1976, the Sex Pistols appeared on the popular UK tea-time chat show *Today*, hosted by Bill Grundy. They were a last-minute replacement for Queen, who had to cancel due to Freddie Mercury's throat infection. The band and their entourage consumed a bottle of Blue Nun in the limo and more liquor in the green room before going on live, unaware the show was unedited. Grundy's provocative questioning led to the band using profanity on air, which resulted in Grundy's two-week suspension, the producer and director's firing, and widespread media outrage with headlines like "the filth and the fury." This 117-second incident, despite being accidental, massively boosted punk rock's profile in the UK, causing "Anarchy in the UK" sales to jump from 10,000 copies in a week to 10,000 copies a day. "The impact of that 117 second interview was immediate."

xref.title: Aer Lingus Air Rage Arrest and Bipolar Diagnosis (2014-2016)
xref.body: On November 10, 2014, Dolores O'Riordan was arrested after a disturbance on Aer Lingus flight 110 from New York to Shannon, about 20 minutes before landing. She was described as irrational and aggressive, injuring a flight attendant, headbutting a police officer, and resisting arrest while proclaiming, "I'm an icon. I'm the queen of Limerick." Transferred to St. Patrick's Psychiatric Hospital, she was diagnosed with bipolar disorder, paranoid and delusional, and stayed for three weeks. She pleaded guilty in December 2015 and was fined $6,600 Canadian on February 24, 2016, with the judge noting her mental illness. The episode was attributed to stress, sleep deprivation, recent separation from her husband of 21 years, and the second anniversary of her father's death. "Dolores has since been diagnosed with bipolar disorder and the stress and sleep deprivation she'd been under triggered an episode."

xref.body: Jeff Healey saw The Trews open for him in Halifax in the summer of 2001 and was impressed. He subsequently offered them a weekly residency as the house band at his new establishment, Jeff Healey's bar, on Bathurst and Queen in Toronto, performing every Thursday. "He really liked us. He said, look, I'm starting a bar called Healey's. You guys give me my house band every Thursday."

xref.title: Rock's First Openly Gay Rock Star
xref.body: Little Richard is argued to be rock's first openly gay rock star, or at least bisexual with strong gay leanings. He openly embraced effeminate mannerisms, wore makeup, engaged in "rough trade," and famously declared, "Elvis may have been the king of rock and roll, but I and the queen." "you can make an argument that he was Rock's first openly gay rock star."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: The "Bohemian Rhapsody" Incident
xref.body: During their tour with Robert Plant, a fan dared The Trews on live radio to perform their old cover of Queen's "Bohemian Rhapsody" at a sold-out show in Rexall Place, Edmonton. The band delivered a "punky version" that garnered a standing ovation. This angered Robert Plant, who, having known Freddie Mercury, didn't want the past relived. He "accosted" their drummer, Sean, the next day in Calgary, but later issued a public apology by praising Canadian songwriters, including The Trews, at the Saddledome. "we got word that we really ticked Robert Plant off."

xref.title: The Acid Queen in "The Who's Tommy"
xref.body: Mary Clayton also ventured into musical theater, appearing on the London stage in the role of the Acid Queen in a production of The Who's "Tommy." This showcases her diverse talents beyond her prolific recording career, demonstrating her versatility as a performer. "Mary has also appeared on the London stage in the role of the acid queen in a production of The Who's Tommy."

xref.title: The Salford Lads' Club Photo Shoot
xref.body: The Smiths posed in front of The Salford Lads' Club, located on Coronation Street in Manchester, for the artwork of their album *The Queen is Dead*. The club, founded in 1904 by Robert Baden Powell, initially disapproved of this appropriation, hiring lawyers to state that the band's music and lyrics were not congruent with their values and that the band was not connected to the club. Despite their unwelcoming stance towards fans recreating the photo, the club eventually lightened up and accepted 20,000 pounds for renovations, recognizing its status as a Smiths shrine. "The Smiths decided to pose there because of the club's history."

xref.title: Tina Bell's Biography
xref.body: Tina Bell passed away in 2012. Her son, an Academy Award-winning documentary director, authored a biography about her titled "Conversations with the Grunge Queen." "If you want to know more about Tina who died in 2012, by the way, there's a biography written by her son called Conversations with the Grunge Queen."

xref.title: Widespread Influence on Artists
xref.body: Grace Jones exerted a significant influence on a diverse range of artists, including Annie Lennox of Eurythmics, Madonna, Lady Gaga, Rihanna, and Lorde. Her impact extends to the drag queen and cross-dressing scene, solidifying her status as a powerful and transformative figure. "Her influence extends not just to follow her, such as any Linux of the Arithmics, but all the way through Madonna, Lady Gaga, Rihanna, and Lord."
